news.title: UBS flags further gold weakness before Fed rate-cut expectations return
Goldman favours gold over silver as central bank demand supports prices
US denies Iranian account that missile damaged F-16 over Gulf
Goldman is out with its 2027 forecast for Brent oil prices
Gold sinks 9% in a week as margin calls and Fed hike bets override its haven role
body: Gold is currently trading as a funding asset, so its near-term direction depends more on equity volatility and leveraged positioning than on traditional safe-haven demand. A December Fed hike is close to fully priced, so further downside from rates alone may be limited. The bigger risk is another wave of liquidation if the AI sell-off deepens. Spot is now far below every major bank's year-end target, so forecast cuts could keep coming, which may weigh on sentiment even if outright selling slows. A sustained halt in equity losses is likely to be the first trigger for bargain hunting.
In this sell-off, gold isn't the shelter. It's one of the first things investors sell to cover losses elsewhere.

Gold has lost its role as a refuge in the current market rout. Bank strategists point to forced selling and rising US rate expectations as the two forces behind its steepest weekly fall in eight months. Spot gold dropped about 2.7% on Friday to around $3,525 an ounce after touching a 14-month low. That left it down roughly 9% on the week and more than a third below its record above $5,500 in January.

ING commodities strategist Ewa Manthey said the macro backdrop had turned against the metal, with higher rate expectations and a firmer US dollar reducing its appeal. She added that the equity sell-off may also have pushed some investors to sell gold to raise cash. Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch also pointed to renewed forced selling as a likely explanation for the latest leg lower.

That pattern is typical of a deleveraging phase. As losses build in leveraged equity positions, particularly in AI-linked stocks, investors sell what they can, not what they want to. Gold's deep liquidity makes it an easy source of cash. The metal kept falling last week even as Treasury yields eased and the dollar's momentum cooled, a sign that liquidation, not rates alone, was doing the damage. Silver fared worse, losing around 14% over the week.

Policy is the other weight. Futures price a December Federal Reserve rate hike as close to certain, and higher rates raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no yield. Goldman Sachs has trimmed its forecasts twice this month because of the Fed's hawkish shift. It sees gold at $4,150 by the end of 2026 and $4,650 by the end of 2027. It still expects a climb above $5,600 in 2028 as investor pressure eases and central bank buying continues.

For now, the outlook depends on the same forces driving stocks. Further equity losses could set off another round of margin-driven selling. Gold will probably need a sign that the Fed is ready to slow its tightening, or a steadier AI trade, before it can rebuild support.

news.title: Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record
body: Goldman's positioning data suggests that last week's rout cleared out mainly the fast money. Mutual funds, ETF buyers and asset managers are still heavily long, which leaves room for more forced or discretionary selling before any bottom forms. A December hike is close to fully priced and no Fed pivot is in sight, so AI earnings news is the most likely of the three catalysts to change the picture. The shift toward a growth downgrade favours defensive sectors and government bonds over cyclicals. It could also weigh on demand-sensitive commodities if it persists.
Hedge funds have already run for the exits, but Goldman's data shows the rest of the market is still long and waiting for a reason to stop selling.

Goldman Sachs has set out three developments that could help mark the bottom of the current US equity correction. It also warned that investor positioning has not fallen far enough yet to signal that the worst is over. In a note from strategist Ben Snider, the bank said any one of three things could support a bottom and recovery. The first is news that lifts confidence in the earnings path tied to AI investment and monetisation. The second is an improvement in the macro backdrop, such as a dovish signal from the Federal Reserve. The third is a significant further drop in investor positioning.

The S&P 500 is now around 12% below its 6 October record, a bigger fall than the median calendar-year peak-to-trough decline of about 10% since 1980. The Nasdaq 100 is down roughly 20%. Snider said the sell-off had widened this week from an AI unwind into a broader growth downgrade. Goldman's AI basket has dropped about 32% since early October, and the S&P 500 excluding AI is now 6% below its high. Cyclical stocks have also started to lag defensives as investors cut their growth expectations. The note's data runs to 19 November, so it predates Friday's steep losses.

On positioning, the picture is mixed. Hedge funds have sold heavily, cutting net leverage to its lowest since April 2025, and their most crowded AI-heavy longs have trailed the S&P 500 by about 14 points over six months. However, Goldman's broader US Equity Sentiment Indicator, which combines nine positioning measures across institutional, retail and foreign investors, stood at 0.7 on 20 November. That is still above average. US equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in close to $170 billion since the start of the fourth quarter, and asset managers' equity futures positioning sits in the 82nd percentile of the past decade.

The Fed route looks the least likely in the near term. Futures price a December hike as close to certain, and Goldman's own economists expect increases in December and March. Goldman's financial conditions index also recorded its sharpest weekly tightening since March 2020.

Goldman's year-ahead outlook, published before the latest slide, targets 8,700 on the S&P 500 by the end of 2027. A newer scenario range runs from roughly 5,800 to 8,100, depending on whether confidence in earnings returns. History offers some support: after 22 corrections of 10% or more since 1980, the index gained an average of 4% over the following three months.

news.title: US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision
body: With a quarter-point hike in December close to fully priced, Bessent's comments mainly push back against the governors (well, one, looking at you Waller!) arguing for 50 basis points. They do little to dislodge 25bp as the base case. If the equity correction deepens, the bigger risk for rate markets is that a hold gets priced back in. For oil, the administration's argument depends on crude-driven inflation fading, so softer energy prices would strengthen Bessent's case and a new spike would back the hawks. Gold has tended to fall on rising hike expectations, so any easing of that pricing could take some pressure off the metal.
With Wall Street in correction and a December decision approaching, the Treasury is now openly arguing that the Fed, not the energy shock, is the bigger risk to the economy.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that the Federal Reserve could damage the economy if it pushes policy too far. In an interview with CBS's Face the Nation, he said many people believe the central bank "may be making a policy mistake if they over-tighten." He pointed to a run of hawkish comments from Fed governors in recent weeks and said financial conditions had tightened substantially over the past few months.

The remarks came as Wall Street slid into correction territory amid a broad sell-off in AI-linked stocks. Bessent gave several explanations for the decline. He said the selling began as Democrats gained ground in the polls and picked up speed after Election Day, arguing that the party's push to slow the AI buildout had unsettled investors. He also named the Fed's tone as a factor. Bessent did not name the officials he had in mind, and he did not say what decision he would like to see from the Fed in December.

Sunday's comments continue an argument Bessent has made throughout November. In a CNBC interview on 13 November, he said it would be a mistake for the Fed to hike too aggressively into an energy supply shock that he said was already easing, and he described recent inflation data as noisy. Speaking to CNBC again on 20 November, he urged policymakers not to back a larger rate rise. He noted that one governor who now favours a 50 basis point increase had supported a cut of a similar size within the past year, and he told the Fed to look forward rather than react to past data.

Bessent's comments reflect the Treasury's view, not that of the officials who set rates. The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point in September to 3.75% to 4.00% and kept it there last month. Some governors are now leaning towards further tightening. Bessent's case is that oil-led price pressure will fade on its own. Fed officials who disagree are more concerned about how long the energy shock keeps inflation high.

The Fed's next decision is 17 days away. Before then, markets will look at incoming inflation data, further Fed commentary and how deep the equity correction goes to judge whether a December hike stays on the table, and how large it might be.

news.title: AUDUSD is the biggest mover of the major currencies this week.  The price falls -2.30% for the week.
body: The AUDUSD is the weakest of the major currencies vs the greenback. It fell -2.3%. The price has now fallen for 10 consecutive days. That move has taken the price from a high on November 10 at 0.69296 to the low today at 0.6609 or -320 pips.

The 320-pip slide in AUDUSD started with a repricing of Fed rate expectations and picked up steam as Australia’s jobs market weakened and the global equity selloff deepened. The Aussie’s 2.30% decline this week, the largest of the seven majors you tracked against the USD, also reflected weakness against other currencies, including the yen and euro.

On the daily chart, AUDUSD broke below 0.6751 earlier this week, taking out the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2025 low. Sellers kept the pressure on, pushing through swing levels at 0.6706 and 0.66588 in succession.

The next downside target is 0.65905, the 50% retracement of that same rally. On a rebound, 0.66588 is the first barometer for buyers. Getting back above that level would take some of the pressure off.

Drilling down to the hourly chart, the AUDUSD selloff started on November 2 with a break below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages. The pair corrected higher on November 4, but by November 5 it was back below both averages. The price has stayed below the lower 100-hour MA ever since.

That 100-hour MA now comes in at 0.67017 and is the first barometer for buyers. They need to get and stay above it to begin to wrestle back some control. If they can do that, the next target is 0.6730, the 38.2% retracement of the move down from the November 9 high. Above that, the 200-hour MA at 0.67586 is the next hurdle.
Until buyers can get and stay above 0.67017, the sellers remain in control on the hourly chart

news.title: Peterson: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means
body: Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.

"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.

The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.

With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.

Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.

Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.

It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of Commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.

The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his long-standing critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.

The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

Andreessen is hugely optimistic about the promise of AI as a technology, but believes the government won't let Americans experience its full effects. Heavy regulation in areas such as healthcare and education mean technology can't replace people's jobs in those sectors, he said.

"To the extent our economy is a free market economy, then maybe you could see the, let's say, extremely rapid displacement scenarios people are talking about," Andreessen said. "But we've mostly outlawed the kind of job transition that … both the utopians the doomers talk about."

news.title: Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran as military warns of strain. FT
body: President Donald Trump is considering new strikes on Iran, the Financial Times reports, as hawkish officials in Washington and Israel urge him to resume military action.

U.S. military planners are warning that American forces risk becoming overextended if the standoff drags into the new year. The warning adds pressure on Trump as he weighs whether to restart strikes and how long U.S. forces can sustain their current posture.

For markets, crude oil is the first place to watch. The report puts escalation risk back in focus, and the next question for traders is whether that risk starts to translate into a bigger premium for potential supply disruptions.

...and there are strains on the world because back on February 28, a war was started with what was thought would be a quick end, but which has proved not be quick at all and the implications are contributing to strains everywhere.
The good news is it took 15 hours to get back to Washington from China, and the President saw his friends.
